title: Alpha/Beta testing your program
summary: Final part of his 'program for yourself' series: run a newly written program through a 2-3 month alpha test that mostly strips out excess, then a long beta test of small tweaks until it becomes a stable, permanent program. He says a self-tested program beats anything bought online.
claims: A written program that hasn't been run is worthless theory; trial and error is unavoidable, and anyone selling a program should have tested it
First self-written programs are almost always too greedy: too many exercises, sets, reps and too much frequency
Common alpha-test problems: exercises that don't suit you, supersets or pairings that fail logistically, and day-to-day sequencing that leaves you fatigued
The alpha test is about stripping things out, not adding (except replacements); new ideas wait for a future program
Don't jump drastically in volume or frequency from your previous novice program (e.g., 3 to 6 days a week at the same daily volume); keep tonnage similar
Decide a target session length before testing; a day planned at 1h15 on paper often takes 2 hours
Log what works after every session, keep an untouched copy of the original program, and run the alpha test for about 2-3 months
Going past about three months of alpha testing risks cutting into the program's skeleton
Aim for the minimum amount of work that yields the maximum results
The beta phase lasts around a year: tweak problem exercises (reps, sets, day, variation) rather than removing them
At the end of beta testing you may realize you can write a better program; build it on the old one's skeleton
A permanent program is defined by flexibility: it adapts to your needs so you can autoregulate without thinking
He beta tested his current plan for two years with about 10-15 tiny changes, one every 1.5-2 months, and now intends to run it indefinitely
In the beta phase only add small things like nucleus overload, three sets of calves or neck, or more forearm work; never add compounds, which would mean starting over
Changes that happen every few days mean the program is chaotic; start from scratch instead
A self-built, beta-tested program is ten times better than one bought from YouTube fitness; naturals must learn to program
He opens with a tribute to Berserk author Kentaro Miura, who just died
